# Documents That Compute {#sec-compute}

```{python}
#| label: ch5-setup
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

from scripts.figures import ACCENT, style

attractions = pd.read_csv("../examples/london/data/attractions.csv")
top = attractions.loc[attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax()]
top_name = top["attraction"]
top_visits = f"{top['visits_2025']:,}"
total_visits = f"{attractions['visits_2025'].sum():,}"
n_free = int(attractions["admission"].str.startswith("Free").sum())
```

So far the guide is text someone typed. This chapter turns it into a document that
*computes*: settings at the top, code that reads the data, numbers in sentences that come from
that code, and a chart that is drawn from the same table. Then one source becomes three
formats, and optionally six, without a single number copied by hand.

This is the chapter where the workflow's central promise becomes concrete. Once a number is
computed rather than typed, correcting the data corrects every place the number appears, in
every format, at the next render. The rest of the book builds on that.

## From `.md` to `.qmd`: YAML front matter {#sec-yaml}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Rename london.md to london.qmd. Replace the "# Visit London" heading with YAML front matter: title "Visit London", author "London Tourism Office", date today, format html. Do not render; my preview rebuilds it.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
renames to `london.qmd` · edits the top of the file
:::

::: {.you}
in the preview tab: Ctrl+C, then `uv run quarto preview london.qmd`
:::

```yaml
---
title: "Visit London"           # <1>
author: "London Tourism Office"
date: today                     # <2>
format: html                    # <3>
---
```
1. `title`, `author` and `date` make the title block, so the old `# Visit London` heading is
   no longer needed.
2. `today` is filled in when the document is rendered.
3. `format` chooses the output; later in this chapter it becomes a list.

*Front matter* is a block of settings between two lines of three dashes at the very top of a
file. It is written in YAML, a format for settings in which indentation is meaning: nested
settings are indented by two spaces, and a wrong indent changes what a setting belongs to.
A `.qmd` file is Markdown plus front matter plus code; the extension tells Quarto to look for
both.

::: pitfall
Delete `london.md` once `london.qmd` exists. Both would write `london.html`, and the one
rendered last wins, so the page you see may not come from the file you edited. Restart the
preview on the new file, too: the old one is still watching `london.md`.
:::

## Code that runs {#sec-code-cells}

::: {.prompt}
```default
In london.qmd, add a Python cell that reads data/attractions.csv and finds the most visited attraction and total visits_2025, plus a sentence showing both with inline code. The preview re-renders it: check london.html.
```
:::

The assistant writes a *code cell*, a code fence whose language is in braces, and a sentence
that uses its results:

````markdown
```{{python}}
import pandas as pd
attractions = pd.read_csv("data/attractions.csv")
top = attractions.loc[attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax()]
top_name = top["attraction"]
top_visits = f"{top['visits_2025']:,}"
total_visits = f"{attractions['visits_2025'].sum():,}"
```

Most visited in 2025: the `{{python}} top_name`, with `{{python}} top_visits` visits.
London's ten most visited ALVA member attractions drew `{{python}} total_visits` visits.
````

When the document renders, the cell runs and its variables are kept; each `` `{{python}} name` ``
is *inline code*, replaced by the value of `name`. Rendered in this book from the same data
file, the sentence reads:

> Most visited in 2025: the `{python} top_name`, with `{python} top_visits` visits. London's
> ten most visited ALVA member attractions drew `{python} total_visits` visits.

Inline code arrived in Quarto 1.4. Before it, a number in a sentence had to be typed, and a
typed number is the one that goes stale (Quarto 1.4 release notes, checked 2026-10-30).

::: practice
**Pause and think.** If `attractions.csv` changes, which numbers in the sentence update?

All three: the top attraction's name, its visits and the total, because each is computed from
the file. They update at the *next render*, not when the file is saved. Anything typed by hand
does not update at all.
:::

The figures come from ALVA's table of visits made in 2025 to its member attractions, retrieved
on 2026-10-30. Only ALVA's members are counted, which is why the sentence says "ALVA member
attractions": the project's rules made the assistant write it that way.

## Cell options: labels, captions and alt text {#sec-cell-options}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Add a matplotlib cell: a horizontal bar chart of visits_2025 by attraction. Hide its code, label it fig-top10, add a caption and alt text. The preview re-renders it: check london.html.
```
:::

Instructions for a cell go in its first lines, as comments that start with `#|`:

```python
#| label: fig-top10                                  # <1>
#| echo: false                                       # <2>
#| fig-cap: "Visits in 2025 (ALVA)."                 # <3>
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of visits by attraction."     # <4>
top10 = attractions.sort_values("visits_2025")
top10.plot.barh(x="attraction", y="visits_2025", legend=False)
```
1. A label starting `fig-` numbers the figure and lets the text refer to it as `@fig-top10`,
   which renders as "Figure 1" with a link.
2. `echo: false` hides the code; readers of a visitor guide want the chart, not the Python.
3. The caption, shown under the figure.
4. The alt text, read aloud by screen readers.

@fig-ldn-top10 is that chart, drawn by this book from the same file. Notice that its caption
and alt text describe different things: the caption says what the chart is, the alt text says
what it shows.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ldn-top10
#| fig-cap: "Visits in 2025 to London's ten most visited ALVA member attractions."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of 2025 visits to ten London attractions, longest bar at the top: the Natural History Museum is highest and Royal Museums Greenwich lowest."
#| classes: on-light
short = attractions.assign(attraction=attractions["attraction"].str.replace(" (South Kensington)", ""))
with style():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.6))
    s = short.sort_values("visits_2025")
    ax.barh(s["attraction"], s["visits_2025"], color=ACCENT)
    ax.set_xlabel("Visits in 2025")
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda x, pos: f"{x / 1e6:.0f}M")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

Matplotlib draws a static image, so the same figure travels to every format: web page, Word,
PDF, slides. Interactive charts, such as Plotly's, are JavaScript that runs in a browser, so
they belong in web pages and dashboards (@sec-audiences) and not in a PDF.

::: tryit
Run the three prompts above, watching the preview after each.

::: done
`london.html` shows the title block, the sentence with computed numbers, and a numbered chart
with a caption and no code.
:::

## One source, three formats {#sec-formats}

::: {.you}
first: Ctrl+C in the preview tab, so that two renders do not collide · restart it afterwards
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
In london.qmd, add docx and typst (label "PDF") formats with download links on the HTML page. Render all three; check each has the computed sentence and chart.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
`uv run quarto render london.qmd` → `london.html` · `london.docx` · `london.pdf`
:::

The front matter's `format` becomes a list:

```yaml
format:
  html:
    format-links:                     # <1>
      - docx
      - {format: typst, text: PDF}     # <2>
  docx: default
  typst: default                       # <3>
```
1. `format-links` adds a download link to the web page for each other format listed.
2. An entry can be a format name, or an object with the format and the link's text.
3. `typst` makes the PDF with the Typst engine inside Quarto; no LaTeX is involved.

One `quarto render` now writes three files. Each format runs the code cells again, so the
inline numbers and the figure appear in every file without anything being copied. To render
only one format, add `--to docx` (or `--to typst`).

::: why
Why render the code once per format? Because a format can change what code produces: a figure
may be drawn at a different size or resolution, and some outputs, such as interactive charts,
only make sense in HTML. Re-running is the price of each format getting output made for it.
For a slow analysis, the cure is to compute once in a script and have every format read the
results, which is exactly how Part III is built (@sec-compute-once).
:::

## Three more formats (optional) {#sec-formats-more}

::: {.prompt}
```default
In london.qmd, add pptx, epub and revealjs (london-slides.html) formats, each with a download link on the HTML page. Render all; check each has the computed sentence and chart.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
`uv run quarto render london.qmd` → six files
:::

```yaml
format:
  html:
    format-links:
      # … docx, PDF
      - pptx
      - epub
      - {format: revealjs, text: Slides}
  pptx: default
  epub: default
  revealjs: {output-file: london-slides.html}     # <1>
```
1. Reveal.js slides are also HTML, so they need their own file name, or they would overwrite
   `london.html`.

In PowerPoint and Reveal.js, each `##` heading becomes a slide. The EPUB is an e-book: open it
in an e-book reader such as Calibre (free, for Windows, macOS and Linux) or Books on a Mac.
This book's EPUB edition is built the same way, with more settings, which @sec-how-built
describes. @fig-render-many shows the render.

![One render, six files: the `format` list in `london.qmd`, a render that runs the code once per format, and the outputs it wrote. ## What a render does, and why two renders collide {#sec-render-mechanics}

@fig-pipeline in @sec-what-quarto showed the three steps of a render. With code in the
document, the first step is worth looking at more closely, because it explains the commonest
failure of this chapter.

To run the cells, Quarto writes the document out as a temporary Jupyter notebook, named after
the file (`london.quarto_ipynb`), starts a Python *kernel* (a running Python process) from the
project's environment, sends it each cell in order, and collects the results. Two
consequences follow. The cells share one Python session, top to bottom, so a later cell can use
a variable from an earlier one, and the order of cells matters. And two renders of the same
file at the same moment write the same temporary files, which is why a render started while a
preview is re-rendering fails with `readfile 'london.quarto_ipynb'`.

Every render runs every cell again. That is deliberate in this book's projects: they set
`freeze: false`, so outputs always match the data. It also means a slow cell slows every
render; @sec-publish-many returns to the trade-off and to `freeze: auto`, which caches results
and needs a rule for when to throw them away.

::: pitfall
Every render prints `[IPKernelApp] WARNING | Kernel is running over TCP without encryption`.
It is harmless: the "TCP" connection is between Quarto and a Python process on your own
computer.
:::

::: tryit
Stop the preview, then add the formats with the prompt in @sec-formats (and, if you like, the
optional three).

::: done
`london.docx` and `london.pdf` show the computed sentence and the chart (and, with the optional
formats, so do the slides, the PowerPoint deck and the e-book).
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

A `.qmd` file is Markdown plus YAML front matter plus code cells. Front matter sets the title
block and the formats, with indentation as meaning. Code cells run at render time in one shared
Python session, and inline code writes their results into sentences, so numbers update when the
data change and nothing typed goes stale. Cell options, written as `#|` comments, label,
caption and describe figures; a `fig-` label makes a figure numbered and referable. One source
renders to HTML, Word and a Typst PDF, and optionally to PowerPoint, an e-book and Reveal.js
slides, each format running the code again. Never run two renders of one file at once.
